provenance: Original authored instructional positions; not historical game records or engine-certified unique best moves.

items.prompt: Find g1 and f3, then move the knight by its coordinates.
items.success: A file and rank uniquely identify the origin and destination.
items.misconception: Do not count files from Black’s perspective.

items.prompt: Move the knight from g1 to f3 even though the board is nearly empty.
items.success: A knight changes two files and one rank and does not need a clear path.
items.misconception: A knight cannot move straight like a rook.

items.prompt: Use the bishop to capture the unprotected pawn on d4.
items.success: The bishop moves diagonally and replaces the pawn on its square.
items.misconception: Moving beside a target does not capture it.

items.prompt: Your king is checked on the d-file. Move it to safety.
items.success: Leaving the rook’s checking file is compulsory before pursuing a plan.
items.misconception: A move that leaves the king on the d-file does not answer check.

items.prompt: Block the long rook check with the bishop.
items.success: A sliding check can be stopped by occupying the line between attacker and king.
items.misconception: Blocking on a square outside the d-file does not stop the check.

items.prompt: Find the rook move that leaves Black’s boxed king no flight square.
items.success: A distant rank check works because Black’s own pawns close the escape squares.
items.misconception: Checkmate requires checking every capture, block and flight square.

items.prompt: Castle kingside after both bishops and knights have developed.
items.success: The king travels two squares and the rook is repositioned only when the corridor is legal.
items.misconception: Do not castle through an attacked square or occupied corridor.

items.prompt: Choose a queen when the b-pawn reaches the last rank.
items.success: Promotion is specified by the new piece, not just the pawn’s destination.
items.misconception: Ending the move on b8 without specifying the promotion piece is incomplete.

items.prompt: Make a legal king move in a bare-kings position.
items.success: Bare kings cannot force mate; the outcome is insufficient material regardless of the move.
items.misconception: A draw is a game outcome, not a license to make an illegal king move.

items.prompt: Capture the free pawn without sacrificing the queen.
items.success: Collect material only after confirming the capturing piece remains safe.
items.misconception: A pawn is worth far less than the queen; do not trade the queen for a pawn.

items.prompt: Capture the pawn that supports Black’s centralized knight.
items.success: The pawn on e5 helps maintain the knight’s square; removing support changes the exchange.
items.misconception: Count the defender and the squares it controls before exchanging.

items.prompt: Trade the rooks on c4 and evaluate the king-and-pawn ending.
items.success: An equal exchange removes activity from both sides; compare the resulting position.
items.misconception: Trading automatically is not enough; inspect what remains afterward.

challenge.prompt: You have an extra queen. Trade the enemy's active rook before pursuing a speculative attack.
challenge.success: A rook exchange removes counterplay and keeps the extra queen. Calculate the material remaining after the trade.
challenge.misconception: Not every trade is good; compare material remaining on the board. Here a rook-for-rook exchange preserves a decisive queen advantage.

successByMove.d1d8: Rxd8+ removes Black's rook while you retain the extra queen. Simplifying is a practical way to convert a clear advantage.

hints: Count what each side owns after the exchange.
Both rooks face one another along the open d-file.
Exchanging the rooks leaves the extra queen on your side.

items.prompt: Develop the position by challenging Black’s central pawn with d4.
items.success: A central pawn advance claims space while creating concrete contact with e5.
items.misconception: Do not copy the model’s e-pawn move when the e-pawn has already advanced.

challenge.prompt: In a Queen's Gambit Declined structure, improve a knight to influence the center; justify the plan.
challenge.success: Both Nc3 and Nf3 develop and increase central influence; they differ in which knight is committed first.
challenge.misconception: Principles are not unique-move rules. Multiple developing moves are playable, but they lead to different move orders and potential structures.

successByMove.b1c3: Nc3 increases central pressure on d5 and develops the queenside knight. Consider how this affects the later e4 break.
successByMove.g1f3: Nf3 develops toward the center, protects d4 and supports future kingside castling while keeping the b1-knight flexible.

hints: Evaluate development and control of d4/e4.
Both knights are still on their home squares.
Choose a knight move and explain the square it newly influences.

items.prompt: Develop a new minor piece toward the center.
items.success: Nc3 increases central control without making unnecessary queen moves.
items.misconception: Re-moving the already developed pawn does not develop a new piece.

challenge.prompt: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6, develop the bishop from f1 without a queen sortie.
challenge.success: Bc4 develops toward f7; Bb5 pressures the c6 knight that supports e5. Both prepare castling.
challenge.misconception: Do not confuse bishop development with a forced attack. Different sound bishop squares lead to different strategic plans.

successByMove.f1c4: Bc4 enters Italian-game structures and eyes f7; prepare central development, not an imaginary immediate mate.
successByMove.f1b5: Bb5 develops in Ruy Lopez fashion and adds positional pressure on the c6 knight; this is not a free capture.

hints: Which undeveloped bishop can leave its home square?
Moving the e-pawn cleared a diagonal for your kingside bishop.
Think of the Italian and Ruy Lopez as different sound plans.

items.prompt: Use the d-pawn to challenge the center rather than moving a wing pawn.
items.success: Central contact matters more than memorizing the model position.
items.misconception: A wing-pawn advance does not contest the e5 pawn immediately.

challenge.prompt: White opened with e4. Challenge the center using direct occupation or pressure on d4.
challenge.success: ...e5 mirrors central occupation; ...c5 creates Sicilian asymmetry and targets d4. Neither is a tactical refutation.
challenge.misconception: Central play is not restricted to occupying e5; flank pressure on d4 can serve a central purpose.

successByMove.e7e5: ...e5 directly occupies the center and frees Black's king bishop, usually leading to open-game development.
successByMove.c7c5: ...c5 attacks the d4-square and creates asymmetry; expect a different pawn structure and concrete theory.

hints: Consider both direct occupation and indirect pressure.
Which pawn can step onto e5 or influence d4?
Both e- and c-pawn moves have established central aims.

items.prompt: Use the now-clear kingside path to castle.
items.success: Castling secures the king and connects the rook to play.
items.misconception: The king is not safe simply because several pieces were developed.

challenge.prompt: Complete king safety in this Italian structure before starting a speculative attack.
challenge.success: O-O removes the king from the center and brings the h1-rook closer to action; verify the castling path first.
challenge.misconception: Castling is not always legal or safe: here both transit squares are clear and unattacked.

successByMove.e1g1: O-O places the king on g1 and rook on f1; neither bishop nor knight blocks the route in this position.

hints: Check the king's starting, transit and arrival squares.
The white bishop and knight have already left f1 and g1.
Move the king two squares toward the rook.

items.prompt: Develop the remaining queenside knight instead of moving the queen repeatedly.
items.success: Completing piece development avoids donating free tempi to the opponent.
items.misconception: Early queen wandering creates targets for developing moves.

challenge.prompt: Continue activating minor pieces instead of repeatedly moving the queen in the opening.
challenge.success: Nf3 fights for e5 and helps castling; Bc4 occupies an active diagonal. Both conserve tempi.
challenge.misconception: Early queen moves may be playable, but premature queen trips can give the opponent free developing attacks.

successByMove.g1f3: Nf3 develops a knight, increases central control and prepares king safety without exposing the queen.
successByMove.f1c4: Bc4 develops along the f7 diagonal; it is positional pressure, not an automatic mating attack.

hints: Which pieces are still on their starting squares?
The king's knight or bishop can join central play.
Choose a minor-piece development that does not require moving the queen.

items.prompt: Develop the knight with a move that also influences e5.
items.success: A useful tempo improves your own piece while applying pressure.
items.misconception: Repeated moves with the same piece often waste opening time.

challenge.prompt: After 1.e4 c5, develop with a coherent Sicilian plan instead of losing time with your queen.
challenge.success: Nf3 often prepares the Open Sicilian d4 break; Nc3 can support a Closed Sicilian setup.
challenge.misconception: A good developing move is not necessarily unique. Its value depends on the central break and pawn structure it serves.

successByMove.g1f3: Nf3 develops and usually supports d4 for Open Sicilian play; determine the timing of that break.
successByMove.b1c3: Nc3 develops while keeping d4 flexible, enabling Closed Sicilian setups. The subsequent piece placement changes.

hints: Identify your intended pawn break.
Both knights can develop without abandoning e4.
Compare an Open Sicilian Nf3 plan with a Closed Sicilian Nc3 plan.

items.prompt: Activate the undeveloped knight toward central squares.
items.success: Nd3 improves reach compared with leaving the knight on the edge of activity.
items.misconception: A piece can be safe but ineffective if it controls no useful squares.

challenge.prompt: Use the empty central file to improve your rook instead of advancing a random flank pawn.
challenge.success: Rd1 gives the rook a useful open-file role. Activity means access to squares and potential targets, not movement for its own sake.
challenge.misconception: An open file is an opportunity rather than an automatic win; check which entry squares or targets can be reached.

successByMove.a1d1: Rd1 moves the rook from a1 to the open d-file, preparing useful central access without claiming immediate material.

hints: Find the file without any pawn.
No piece blocks the first-rank path from a1 to d1.
Bring the a1-rook to d1.

items.prompt: Improve the least active knight while preserving the pawn.
items.success: Moving the idle knight is more productive than moving the active king without purpose.
items.misconception: Fix the worst piece rather than making the best piece even better.

challenge.prompt: Improve an undeveloped knight after 1.e4 c5; choose between Open and Closed Sicilian plans.
challenge.success: Both knights are undeveloped. Nf3 and Nc3 both improve your position, but their follow-up plans differ.
challenge.misconception: The worst piece is not a fixed square. Focus on mobility, threats and the intended pawn structure before selecting a route.

successByMove.g1f3: Nf3 develops actively and often prepares the d4 break in an Open Sicilian.
successByMove.b1c3: Nc3 develops and keeps the d-pawn flexible, commonly favoring a Closed Sicilian structure.

hints: Look for pieces still at home.
Two knights have sensible centralizing squares.
Choose a route that matches the structure you intend to play.

items.prompt: Create a bishop check with the queen behind the king on the same diagonal.
items.success: Bf6+ attacks the king first; after it moves the queen on h8 becomes vulnerable.
items.misconception: In a skewer the more valuable piece is attacked first, not the piece behind it.

items.prompt: Remove the knight defending key squares near the black king.
items.success: Bxf6 eliminates a defender before trying a direct king attack.
items.misconception: Attacking the king while leaving its key defender is often premature.

items.prompt: Use the rook on the e-file to force Black’s defenders to react.
items.success: Rxe8+ demands a response and can draw the queen away from its original defensive job.
items.misconception: A quiet move fails to challenge the overloaded back-rank defender.

items.prompt: Force a recapture that pulls the queen onto a less useful square.
items.success: Rxe8+ changes the queen’s task and square through a forcing exchange.
items.misconception: A decoy is not any capture: identify where the defender must go.

items.prompt: Put direct pressure on the rook that the queen must also defend.
items.success: The forcing rook capture makes Black commit its multipurpose defender.
items.misconception: An overloaded piece cannot satisfy all defensive duties at once.

items.prompt: Move the bishop aside to uncover the rook’s e-file.
items.success: Bf3 removes the friendly obstruction from the line to the black king.
items.misconception: A discovered line cannot function while your own piece blocks it.

items.prompt: Choose the central pawn break before another routine developing move.
items.success: Opening the center now changes the sequence of forcing responses.
items.misconception: Check forcing moves and captures before deciding an opening move order.

challenge.prompt: Down a queen, calculate checks first. Find the drawing resource and verify the recapture after ...Kd8.
challenge.success: Nd6+ forks king and queen; after ...Kd8 Nxc8 Kxc8, the board has bare kings and is a draw. Never stop calculation at 'wins queen'.
challenge.misconception: Tactical success depends on the entire forced sequence. A queen capture does not win if the opponent's king recaptures your final knight.

successByMove.f5d6: Nd6+ is a drawing fork, not a material win: ...Kd8 Nxc8 Kxc8 leaves bare kings.

hints: Calculate every check and reply.
The knight can fork the king on e8 and queen on c8.
After ...Kd8 Nxc8, see whether Black's king recaptures.

items.prompt: Penetrate with the rook on the open b-file.
items.success: Rb8+ uses an uncontested file and the eighth rank to create a threat.
items.misconception: A rook cannot penetrate through its own pawn chain.

challenge.prompt: Both d-pawns are absent. Claim the open file for future rook activity.
challenge.success: Rd1 centralizes the rook on an unblocked file and improves its access to Black's camp.
challenge.misconception: Occupying an open file is not proof of a forced gain. The advantage depends on entry squares and future piece coordination.

successByMove.a1d1: Rd1 puts the rook on the open d-file. Next evaluate where it may penetrate and what Black can contest.

hints: Find a file without pawns.
The d-file is clear from d1 to d8.
The a1 rook can cross b1 and c1 to d1.

items.prompt: Use the stable knight post to jump toward Black’s king.
items.success: Nc7+ exploits the knight’s central placement and creates a concrete threat.
items.misconception: An outpost matters only if it supports useful future operations.

challenge.prompt: Improve the knight onto a protected central outpost Black cannot readily chase with a pawn.
challenge.success: Nd5 is protected by the e4 pawn; Black has no c- or e-pawn to drive it away from that square.
challenge.misconception: An advanced knight is not necessarily an outpost. Check whether an enemy pawn can challenge its destination.

successByMove.c3d5: Nd5 takes the central outpost supported by e4; Black may seek an exchange of pieces but lacks a pawn challenge.

hints: Look for a square defended by your e-pawn.
There is no black c- or e-pawn to attack d5.
Jump from c3 to d5.

items.prompt: Advance the e-pawn to confront Black’s locked center.
items.success: e5 changes the pawn contact and challenges the fixed d5 structure.
items.misconception: A pawn break must change contact with the opponent’s pawns.

challenge.prompt: Open the center by exchanging the c-pawn for Black's d-pawn; calculate the recapture.
challenge.success: cxd5 opens the c-file, but ...exd5 can restore a black pawn on d5. Evaluate the structure, not an imaginary material win.
challenge.misconception: A central capture is a structural decision. A pawn break often changes open files and weak squares without gaining material.

successByMove.c4d5: cxd5 clears the c-file and forces Black to consider ...exd5. Study the resulting pawn chain before judging the trade.

hints: Find central pawn contact.
White's c4 pawn attacks d5.
Check Black's e6-pawn recapture after cxd5.

items.prompt: Bring the king toward the fixed isolated pawn on d7.
items.success: King activation targets a pawn that cannot retreat.
items.misconception: Do not chase a target with only one piece while abandoning king activity.

challenge.prompt: Black's d5-pawn has no c- or e-pawn partner. Apply long-range pressure with your rook.
challenge.success: Rd1 puts pressure on the isolated pawn. It is a starting plan, not an immediately forced pawn win.
challenge.misconception: A weakness can be defended. Do not claim that attacking an isolated pawn automatically wins it; build pressure and calculate defenses.

successByMove.a1d1: Rd1 attacks the isolated d5-pawn down an open file and gives White a clear strategic target.

hints: Identify the isolated pawn.
The d-file has no blocking pawn in front of your rook.
Place the rook on d1 to pressure the target.

items.prompt: Exploit the trapped king immediately with a long rook check.
items.success: Ra8# works because the king has no safe escape across the back rank.
items.misconception: An attack is justified by concrete king geometry, not optimism.

items.prompt: Use the fully open a-file to invade with check.
items.success: An uncontested file is a route to the enemy eighth rank.
items.misconception: Do not divert the rook from an open line without a concrete gain.

items.prompt: Remove the knight shielding the king-side squares.
items.success: Bxf6 changes the number of useful defenders around Black’s king.
items.misconception: Count real defenders before starting a speculative assault.

items.prompt: Seal the back rank with a rook check against the boxed king.
items.success: Ra8# works because the black pawns cover their own king’s exits.
items.misconception: A checking move is only mate after every flight is excluded.

items.prompt: Choose the forcing bishop check that wins a queen, not a speculative sacrifice.
items.success: Bf6+ skewers the exposed king and queen; the concrete line matters.
items.misconception: If a sacrifice lacks a calculated return, reject it in favor of forcing value.

items.prompt: Consider h3 as preventive space against a future bishop pin.
items.success: A prophylactic pawn move can ask a developing bishop to declare its intentions.
items.misconception: Prophylaxis only helps if the opponent really has a relevant idea.

challenge.prompt: The knight on c6 could jump to b4, hitting c2. Use a pawn move to discourage ...Nb4.
challenge.success: a3 guards b4 without moving the c-pawn; c3 also controls b4 and moves the pawn from c2. Both have structural costs.
challenge.misconception: Prophylaxis requires a concrete threat. Here the point is ...Nb4; choose which pawn commitment suits the rest of your position.

successByMove.a2a3: a3 controls b4 with the a-pawn while retaining c2, at the cost of a move.
successByMove.c2c3: c3 controls b4 and removes the pawn target from c2, but restricts the c3-square for your own pieces.

hints: Visualize the knight after ...Nb4.
From b4 it would attack the c2-pawn.
Either a- or c-pawn can guard b4.

items.prompt: Eliminate the active rook on c4 through a direct exchange.
items.success: Rxc4 removes the piece exerting the immediate pressure.
items.misconception: Trading a passive defender does not remove the attacker.

items.prompt: Find a forcing check that makes the exposed king answer you immediately.
items.success: Qf8+ checks along the eighth rank and makes Black respond rather than continue a plan.
items.misconception: Counterplay must create an actual threat, not just move a piece toward the king.

items.prompt: Use the queen to cut the king’s available squares from a safe distance.
items.success: Qf6+ reduces the box without putting the queen beside the king.
items.misconception: Rushing close to the king can invite stalemate or lose coordination.

items.prompt: Deliver the rank check against the boxed king.
items.success: Ra8# demonstrates the rook’s horizontal cut-off.
items.misconception: A rook alone cannot mate without the king or board-edge confinement.

items.prompt: Advance the king toward the opponent while preserving pawn support.
items.success: Ke5 approaches the critical central squares without abandoning the pawn.
items.misconception: Opposition is about king geometry, not copying a pawn move.

items.prompt: Move your king toward the pawn’s important entry squares.
items.success: Kd3 helps the king approach the key squares in front of the d-pawn.
items.misconception: The pawn needs king support; advancing it without the king can lose tempi.

items.prompt: Exchange active rooks before entering the remaining endgame.
items.success: Rxc4 removes the tactical counterplay and simplifies material.
items.misconception: Simplification works only if the resulting ending remains favorable.

items.prompt: Make the routine improving move without overthinking.
items.success: Nf3 develops and adds immediate central control.
items.misconception: Use more time on irreversible tactical decisions than on standard development.

items.prompt: Select a workable plan: develop a new piece to influence the center.
items.success: Nc3 is a concrete improvement rather than a vague aspiration.
items.misconception: A plan should identify an actual improving move.

challenge.prompt: In this Italian position, prepare a sensible central plan with one quiet pawn move.
challenge.success: d3 reinforces e4 and favors a restrained setup; c3 supports the later d4 break. Both need further development and king safety.
challenge.misconception: A single quiet pawn push is not an entire plan. Explain the follow-up and calculate Black's response before starting a central break.

successByMove.d2d3: d3 supports e4 and creates a measured Italian structure. Prepare castling and later central play.
successByMove.c2c3: c3 prepares the later d4 pawn advance. Complete development and calculate whether Black can strike centrally.

hints: Ask what central pawn advance you want next.
Supporting e4 and preparing d4 are both legitimate aims.
Consider either d3 or c3, with distinct follow-up plans.

items.prompt: Complete king safety before planning the middlegame.
items.success: Castling marks the transition from opening priorities to piece coordination.
items.misconception: Do not start a flank plan while your king remains unnecessarily exposed.

items.prompt: The last move gave check on the d-file. Re-scan and reply legally.
items.success: Kc1 is safe and reflects the changed threat after the opponent’s move.
items.misconception: An old plan can become illegal after a check.

items.prompt: Recover from a mistake by first saving the attacked queen.
items.success: Qe3 stops the immediate material loss; stabilize before counterattacking.
items.misconception: Do not chase compensation while leaving a queen en prise.
